newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish police step up anti-IRA searches.
newsitem.headline: Irish police step up anti-IRA searches.

text.p: Irish police stepped up search operations on Wednesday after raids that Irish media said had foiled planned IRA bombings in British Northern Ireland.
Four people detained on Tuesday after the seizure of vital bomb parts were still being questioned, police said.
"Searches are still continuing in four counties," a security source told Reuters.

The discovery of quantities of home-made detonating cord packed with powerful semtex commercial explosives was hailed as "a bodyblow to IRA (Irish Republican Army) terrorist plans" by the Irish Independent newspaper.
According to the Irish Times, the operation "disrupted a major arms supply route into Northern Ireland" where the guerrillas are waging an armed campaign against British rule.

"One of the men arrested in County Kildare is suspected of controlling a long-established arms supply route. He is regarded as being a senior IRA member and has close links with a prominent IRA family from east (County) Tyrone," the Irish Times said.
The detonating cord is similar to that used in IRA bomb attacks on British targets in Northern Ireland, England and Germany last year, security sources said.
The Irish Times said that "the disruption to the IRA's operation could make the latest Garda (police) find one of the most important in several years."
IRA guerrillas have carried out a 28 year war to reunite Northern Ireland with Ireland.

Britain and Ireland, who are trying to ease tension between the province's pro-British majority Protestants and Irish minority Catholics, say the guerrillas must abandon violence to win a voice in peace talks.
Last week a British soldier was shot dead at a checkpoint near the frontier with Ireland and the IRA was widely blamed.
The guerrillas, who have made no comment on the shooting, say they will not consider a ceasefire before Britain has a new government in an election to be held by May.

John Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's moderate Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party, on Wednesday spurned a bid by the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm for an electoral pact aimed at giving nationalists more seats in the British parliament.

Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin had urged the SDLP to end opposition to an alliance, saying nationalists could double their representation by winning up to eight of the region's 18 parliamentary seats.
Hume said that if the SDLP made a pact "with a party that is still committed to what they call the 'armed struggle', it would damage our reputation all over the world".
